title: How fast does one electron go?
hook: A lamp lights the moment you flip its switch. So how quick are the electrons?

knows: a lamp lights the moment you switch it on
doesNotKnow: that each electron drifts at well under a millimetre a second
that the lamp lights at once because the wire is already full of electrons that all start moving together

misconception: Electrons rush from the switch to the bulb almost at the speed of light.
objective: The learner can explain that each electron in a lamp's wire drifts at well under a millimetre a second, so it takes hours to cross 2 m, and that the lamp still lights at once because the wire is already full of free electrons that all start moving together.

claims.text: The drift speed of the electrons in a wire is v = I / (n A e): current divided by (free electrons per cubic metre × cross-section × electron charge).
claims.source: Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, chapter on current and resistance (current density J = n e v_d). artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs (main checkout), block '56 electron-speed-in-a-wire'. Demo.tsx V_DRIFT. Brief claim 1.

claims.text: Copper has about 8.5×10²⁸ free electrons per cubic metre (one per atom: 8,960 kg/m³ ÷ 0.06355 kg/mol × 6.022×10²³ = 8.49×10²⁸); the stage's faint dots stand for these electrons, already in the wire before the switch closes (dots drawn far sparser than real).
claims.source: check.mjs block 56 (nCu = 8.491e28). Demo.tsx N_CU. Brief claim 2.

claims.text: At 1 A in 1 mm² copper the drift is 0.073 mm/s: the tinted electron moves 0.07 mm in 1 s, 4.4 mm in 1 min and 26 cm in 1 h, and the 2 m trip from switch to bulb takes 7.6 h (stage marker labels '+0.07 mm', '+4.4 mm', '+26 cm'; label '2 m trip: 7.6 h'; Seen row '1 min: 4.4 mm · 1 h: 26 cm · trip: 7.6 h'; reveal: 'crept only 4.4 mm in a minute and 26 cm in an hour: the 2 m trip takes 7.6 h', 'about 0.07 mm a second').
claims.source: v = 1 / (8.5e28 × 1e-6 × 1.602e-19) = 7.34e-5 m/s; ×60 = 4.41 mm; ×3600 = 26.4 cm; 2 / v = 27,240 s = 7.57 h. check.mjs block 56. Demo.tsx computes every label from V_DRIFT. Brief claim 3.

claims.text: The lamp lights the moment the switch closes: the push (the electric field) travels along the wire at a large fraction of light speed, about 10 ns (10 billionths of a second) for 2 m here, taking about 2×10⁸ m/s as an illustrative value (hook 'A lamp lights the moment you flip its switch'; stage label 'lit after ~10 ns'; Seen row 'lit: ~10 ns'; reveal 'Your bulb lit about 10 ns (10 billionths of a second) after the switch').
claims.source: Purcell and Morin, Electricity and Magnetism, on fields in conductors and transmission lines (signal speed set by the wire's surroundings, typically 0.5 to 0.9 c). check.mjs block 56 (2 / 2e8 = 10 ns, illustrative). Brief claim 4: 'about' is stated.

claims.text: The wire is already full of free electrons, and closing the switch pushes on all of them at once, so the ones inside the bulb start moving straight away; all of them drift together at the same speed (stage: every faint dot shifts by the same distance as the tinted one; reveal: 'The faint dots are the wire's free electrons, there all along. Closing the switch pushed on all of them at once, so the ones in the bulb moved straight away').
claims.source: Halliday, Resnick and Walker, chapter on current and resistance (the same current, so the same drift speed, in every part of a uniform series loop; current-same-around-loop). Demo.tsx moves every dot by the same displacement.

claims.text: Idealisations: a steady 1 A DC current from a battery in 1 mm² copper wire, with the 2 m route from switch to bulb drawn shorter than real and the first 30 cm of it drawn as a ruler under the circuit (stage caption '1 A in 1 mm² copper wire. Tinted dot: one electron.'). Electrons leave the battery's negative terminal, so they drift from the switch towards the bulb. Not on the stage: on AC mains the electrons only jiggle back and forth and never make the trip.
claims.source: Brief claim 5. Demo.tsx PX_M (100 px per m on the circuit) and RX_CM (9.33 px per cm on the ruler).

recall.question: Electrons in a lamp's wire move slower than a snail. Why does the light still come on the instant you flip the switch?
options: The electrons speed up to near light speed when the switch closes
The wire is already full of electrons, and all of them start moving together
The bulb stores electrons from last time it was on
recall.why: Each electron only drifts, well under a millimetre a second, but the wire is full of them. Closing the switch pushes on all of them at once, so the ones in the bulb move straight away.
